title: Characterisation of a satellite-to-ground channel for continuous variable quantum key distribution protocol
authors: Emma Tien Hwai Medlock, Vinod N. Roa, Timothy Spiller, Rupesh Kumar
abstract: In space based quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, the quantum channel will be dynamic in nature and the channel loss will change with respect to the zenith angle. In the context of continuous variable (CV)-QKD, this will cause issues with parameter estimation and for a transmitted local oscillator in particular it will also fluctuate the shot noise. Therefore, it is vital to characterise this channel loss and the sources of this loss. In this paper the varying channel loss is characterised under practical assumptions. This is shown for various different scenarios, turbulence strengths, as well as wavelengths. This work shows, for the channel parameters considered, it is possible to generate a positive secret key if restricted Eve security assumptions are made.
summary: This paper characterizes the complex, variable channel loss encountered when performing Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution from a satellite to Earth due to atmospheric turbulence and beam spreading. By modeling these physical impairments across different zenith angles, the authors demonstrate that secure quantum key generation remains feasible under specific operational constraints.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing dynamic channel loss for Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution (CV-QKD) when transmitting signals from a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite to a ground station.
main_result: It demonstrates that by characterizing variable channel losses due to atmospheric effects like turbulence and beam wandering, it is possible to generate a positive secret key rate under restricted security assumptions for the proposed space-based QKD link.
method: The analysis involves modeling atmospheric propagation using established models (e.g., Hufnagel-Andrew-Phillips) to calculate weighted averages of refractive index structure parameters ($C_N^2$), alongside detailed calculations for scintillation variance and beam spreading loss.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a satellite-to-ground free-space optical link operating at 1550 nm, utilizing the parameters derived from the SPOQC mission concept. The analysis incorporates effects like atmospheric attenuation, turbulence-induced broadening, and pointing inaccuracies.
key_observables: Achievable secret key rates, weighted $C_N^2$ profiles vs. zenith angle, scintillation variance ($\sigma^2_{	ext{sci}}(	heta)$), and total loss due to various atmospheric impairments.
important_parameters: Zenith angles between $-30^\circ$ and $+30^\circ$, LEO altitude (550 km), wavelength (1550 nm), and varying turbulence strengths ($C_N^2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on practical assumptions, restricted Eve security assumptions, and models the channel loss based on specific atmospheric propagation equations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the satellite pass geometry over the ground station. Figure 2 shows profiles of $C_N^2$ versus altitude (top) and weighted $C_N^2$ versus zenith angle (bottom).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of characterizing dynamic loss in space-based CV-QKD. It then details the physical modeling of atmospheric effects, including turbulence and beam spreading across various zenith angles. Finally, it presents the derived key rate analysis based on these characterized channel parameters.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous theoretical framework for quantifying decoherence and loss mechanisms (scintillation, wandering) in real-world, dynamic free-space quantum channels. The integration of atmospheric physics into QKD security analysis is key.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Satellite pass over the OGS. Here, the CV-QKD exchange occurs between zenith angles −30◦and +30◦. For this scenario, the satellite will have an altitude of 550 km.

Figure 2: C2 N profiles as a function of altitudes (shown on the top) and the weighted C2 N profile for 550 km downlink as a function of zenith angles (shown on the bottom). Here the power law parameter for day time pday = 1.33 was used, random background turbulence parameter M = 1, root-mean-square high altitude wind speed vw = 21 m/s, and with the initial turbulence strengths as seen in the parameter table.
Figure 3: Point ahead angle for a given satellite altitude. The PAA changes with increasing altitudes of the satellite, ranging from 250 km to 2000 km. This is a typical range for LEO satellites.

Figure 4: Total upper bound channel loss with differing receiver aperture sizes. This was done for a strong turbulence regime, with a wavelength of 1550 nm, a transmitter aperture of 8 cm, a pointing error at the satellite of 4 µrad, and with the satellite at an altitude of 550 km.

Figure 5: The losses as a dependency of wavelength at the zenith is plotted. Here the atmospheric absorption lines have not been taken into consideration. The losses are plotted for a receiver aperture of 60 cm with 30% obstruction, a transmitter aperture of 8 cm, a pointing error at the satellite of 4 µrad, and with the satellite at an altitude of 550 km. This is the loss for a Gaussian modulated CV (GMCV) QKD protocol. For DV-QKD, there will be additional losses due to phase error [50–52] that GMCV does not need to consider as the transmitted local oscillator will experience the same phase drift as the quantum signal [53–55].
